stories.title: Six Chinese nationals among seven killed in Russian gas plant fire
stories.summary: Six Chinese nationals were killed and nine more are missing after a fire broke out at a gas chemical complex in Russia's far eastern Amur region, the plant said on Wednesday. A total of seven people died and 152 people were treated for injures, including 36 who were rushed to hospitals, the plant said on the Telegram messaging app on Wednesday. The fire, which broke out on Tuesday, was extinguished, it added. An emergency services plane had arrived to transport the injured to other hospitals in Russia. The complex, which bills itself as one of the world's largest polyethylene and polypropylene producers, is a joint project of Russian company Sibur and Chinese oil and gas company Sinopec. It has yet to begin operations and was preparing for production start. Russia frequently relies on foreign labour, including workers from China, for the construction of large industrial and infrastructure projects. Russia's Investigative Committee said it was investigating the incident as a potential breach of industrial safety regulations and was working to establish the cause of the fire.

stories.title: 'Magical' and rare barn owl has bumper breeding season
stories.summary: Barn owls have had a bumper summer in County Fermanagh, with 10 chicks recorded across two sites. The breeding success follows years of conservation work by Ulster Wildlife with local farmers installing nest boxes and improving habitat for the elusive bird. There are thought to be fewer than 30 breeding pairs left in Northern Ireland. The chicks have had rings placed on their legs so that they can be recorded in any other areas they turn up in after leaving the nest. People are being encouraged to report any sightings of barn owls across Northern Ireland, particularly in the west, to help fill in gaps in the records and even help protect important breeding areas. The Fermanagh chicks are thought to be the first recorded ones in the county for half a century. Most of Ulster Wildlife's barn owl records come from the east of Northern Ireland. The two broods of five chicks appeared in nest boxes that had been installed at different sites, after more than a decade of work with landowners. The locations are being kept secret to help protect the rare, locally endangered bird. Katy Bell, a senior conservation officer from Ulster Wildlife, said nest boxes play a part, but the willingness of farmers to adapt to the needs of the "magical, mystical" barn owl has been important too. "We've been working closely with landowners, advising on land management and also putting up boxes," she said. "So it's the combination of both - really you need nice thick hedgerows, lots of kind of rough areas and long grass for them to hunt over and then somewhere for them to nest.
